newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan food firm says officials in suspected payoff.
newsitem.headline: Japan food firm says officials in suspected payoff.

text.p: A leading Japanese maker of food and seasonings, Ajinomoto Co, said on Tuesday that two of its executives had been arrested on suspicion of paying several million yen in company funds to "sokaiya" racketeers.

Company president Shunsuke Inamori told a news conference that the two senior officials belonged to the firm's general affairs department, but stressed that neither he nor other top managers had been involved in payoffs.
The new scandal follows revelations last week of suspected illegal dealings and possible payoffs to a one-time racketeer by Japan's biggest brokerage, Nomura Securities.

Inamori said Ajinomoto director Yukio Noguchi, 60, who was head of its general affairs department, and Takao Ishigami, 48, a section chief in the department, were suspected of paying the money to six sokaiya racketeers to ensure that a shareholders' meeting held last June would run smoothly.
Ishigami, a former police officer, was in charge of dealing with sokaiya, but in-house auditing had not been carried out until the beginning of this year, company officials said.

Sokaiya, often linked to "yakuza" crime syndicates, typically try to extort money from firms by threatening to expose dubious business practices or to make a disturbance at shareholders' meetings -- called "sokai" in Japanese.
Companies have also been known to hire sokaiya to muzzle legitimate shareholders' questions at the meetings.
Japanese law has prohibited payoffs to them since 1982.
"We take the case very seriously. We apologise for upsetting the public," Inamori said. "Everything is not yet clear so we need an in-house investigation."

Asked what kind of action he might take to atone for the suspected payoffs, Inamori said: "I will consider this (what I should do) after the investigation is completed, but this is a separate issue from the question of whether I should resign."
Asked whether the company's top management including himself had been involved in any payoffs he flatly denied such a possibility. "I have not been involved," he said.

Ajinomoto was one of several companies accused in the United States of fixing the price of lysine, a feed additive. It pleaded guilty and agreed to pay a fine of $10 million, a spokesman for the U.S. Attorney in Chicago said last November.
Asked whether the arrests in the sokaiya case would have any adverse effect on the company's sales, Inamori said: "I think so, but I'm not sure."

In June last year, the president of prestigious Japanese department store Takashimaya Co Ltd resigned to take management responsibility for the arrest of a former executive and two officials on suspicion of payoffs to sokaiya.
The former officials pleaded guilty to the charges last November.
